title: Text and Language
full_title: Text, Tokens and Classical Language Models
tagline: Text as data, tokenisation, n-gram language models, perplexity and word embeddings
summary: A language model assigns probabilities to text. This course starts from text as data, builds tokenisers, n-gram language models and their evaluation by perplexity, and learns word embeddings — the ideas on which neural language models are built.
overview: Long before a neural network is trained, a language model depends on choices about text itself — what counts as a symbol, how text is cut into tokens, how predictions are scored — and those choices shape everything after. This course studies text as data and the classical language models that came before neural networks: the statistics of words, tokenisers from words to bytes, n-gram models and smoothing, perplexity, and word embeddings learned from co-occurrence.

The course follows the pipeline of a modern model in miniature. Text arrives as Unicode characters and is segmented by a tokeniser, usually a subword method such as byte-pair encoding; an n-gram model estimates the probability of each token from the few before it, and perplexity measures how well it predicts held-out text. Distributional semantics turns co-occurrence counts into vectors, word2vec and GloVe learn them efficiently, and simple classifiers built on such representations solve tasks such as sentiment and topic classification. A last chapter introduces the linguistic structure — morphology, syntax and meaning — that classical NLP made explicit and large models learn implicitly.

The ideas are elementary but their consequences are not: tokenisation explains why models struggle to count letters and why some languages cost more tokens than others, and the sparsity of n-gram counts is the problem that neural language models solved. Build each model yourself on a small corpus; watching a trigram model generate text is good preparation for the rest of the atlas.
outcomes: Describe text as data — Unicode, characters and words — and the statistical regularities of language such as Zipf’s law.
Implement and compare tokenisers, including byte-pair encoding, WordPiece, unigram and byte-level tokenisers.
Build n-gram language models with smoothing, and generate text from them.
Evaluate language models by cross-entropy, perplexity and bits per byte, and compare models with different tokenisers fairly.
Explain distributional semantics, train word embeddings with word2vec or GloVe, and interpret the geometry of embedding spaces.
Build text classifiers from bag-of-words features and embeddings.
Describe morphology, syntax and semantics, and the classical NLP tasks of tagging, parsing and named-entity recognition.

history.title: Markov’s chains of letters
history.detail: Markov counted vowels and consonants in the first 20,000 letters of Pushkin’s *Eugene Onegin* and showed that each letter depends on the one before — the first Markov chain applied to language.

history.title: Zipf’s law
history.detail: In *The Psycho-Biology of Language* Zipf documented that a word’s frequency is roughly inversely proportional to its rank, which makes most words rare in any corpus.

history.title: The entropy of English
history.detail: Shannon asked people to guess the next letter of a text and estimated that printed English carries roughly one bit per letter — an early version of the bits-per-character that language models now report.

history.title: The distributional hypothesis
history.detail: Harris argued that words occurring in similar contexts have similar meanings; Firth’s 1957 slogan ‘You shall know a word by the company it keeps’ made the idea famous.

history.title: Kneser–Ney smoothing
history.detail: Kneser and Ney smoothed n-gram estimates by backing off to how many different contexts a word appears in, the best-performing n-gram method in later comparisons.

history.title: A neural probabilistic language model
history.detail: Bengio and colleagues replaced n-gram counts with a neural network over learned word vectors, attacking the curse of dimensionality that limits n-gram models.

history.title: word2vec
history.detail: Mikolov and colleagues trained word embeddings with the skip-gram and CBOW objectives on billions of words, and showed that vector arithmetic captures analogies such as king − man + woman ≈ queen.

history.title: GloVe
history.detail: Pennington, Socher and Manning fitted word vectors to global co-occurrence statistics, connecting prediction-based embeddings with matrix factorisation.

history.title: Subword units
history.detail: Sennrich, Haddow and Birch adapted byte-pair encoding, a 1994 compression algorithm by Gage, to split rare words into subwords for neural machine translation — the tokenisation method of most language models since.
